notes.title: Recognition brings hostility with it
notes.body: 油然而生 describes a feeling arising spontaneously. In his April 2025 Dazed interview, Jackzebra said the hostility toward him had increased alongside his audience. That is useful context for this verse’s move from coming first to attracting hate, without identifying any one person as its target.

notes.title: The taste of envy
notes.body: 酸 means sour, but it also describes envy in Chinese internet speech: someone else's success can leave a sour taste. The lyric pushes that taste into an exaggerated bodily image—sour enough to make your teeth fall out—immediately after boasting about coming first and attracting hate.

sources.label: People's Daily Overseas Edition: internet slang, 2019

phrase.en: so sour your teeth fall out

notes.title: Book, title, words
notes.body: The next three images all belong to writing: a book, its title and its words. They become deep-fried, withered and insecure. Read as a sequence, they turn contempt into a grotesque little portrait of a text. The book itself is unnamed.

notes.title: Hehe. Not hehe.
notes.body: 嘻嘻 / 不嘻嘻 is a Chinese internet meme built around a sudden reversal: laughing a moment ago, then no longer laughing. Southern Weekly explained the paired expression in July 2024. Here it follows graphic threats, turning a familiar comic mood-switch into a taunt.

sources.label: Southern Weekly / Nanfang Plus: the 嘻嘻不嘻嘻 meme, July 2024

notes.title: Looking down, twice
notes.body: The song begins above the earth, looking down on everything; 瞧不起 then means regarding somebody as beneath you. English “look down on” preserves this movement from physical elevation to social contempt. The broad aerial view narrows into a refusal to recognize one particular “you.”

notes.title: A heart can move two ways
notes.original: 我才不管你心会动不动
notes.body: 心动 commonly means being emotionally stirred or attracted. This line spreads those words around a verb for possibility: a heart that may or may not move. After the dismissal of another person's pain, 'still beats' emphasizes bodily menace, while an emotional echo remains available in Chinese.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 心動

notes.title: A double negative that demands respect

phrase.en: no choice but to give me my due

notes.body: 服 here means accepting someone’s ability or superiority, not merely obeying. 不服不行 literally says that refusing to acknowledge it will not do: the listener is denied even the option of withholding respect. It is a sharper boast than simply saying “I am good.”

notes.title: Warmth inside the clique
notes.body: The literal image is bodies grouping together against the cold. Here it sits beside “losers” and the next line’s resource-swapping, making mutual support sound like a closed circle protecting itself. The same phrase returns beside “little cliques” in “Monoplay.”

notes.title: A swear word can be praise
notes.body: 牛逼 is vulgar praise for being impressive, formidable, or exceptionally good. Translating its component characters literally would lose the meaning. Its approving force also contrasts with the abusive 狗逼 earlier in the song: compounds containing 逼 do not all carry the same judgment.

notes.title: Showing your hand
notes.body: 摊牌 means laying your cards face up, and by extension revealing your position or what you have been keeping back. 我不装了 adds 'I'm done pretending.' Together they make a theatrical reveal: the repeated boasts are now out in the open.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 攤牌

phrase.en: Cards on the table, I'm done pretending

notes.title: The opening comes from “Nettles”
notes.original: Maybe you're right and we should stop watchin' the news (men—)
notes.body: The intro quotes Ethel Cain’s “Nettles” (2025). Cain recites these same two sung lines in her own Genius Verified breakdown. Discussing that song, she describes love becoming frightening because there is now someone to lose. That context sits beside this song’s opening fear of losing everything, before Jack turns toward gratitude and protecting the people close to him.

sources.label: Ethel Cain explains and recites Nettles — Genius Verified

notes.title: Brown eyes that look blue
notes.original: 'Cause, baby, I've never seen brown eyes look so blue
notes.body: “Blue” means sad as well as the color. The eyes remain brown; what changes is the grief visible in them. The color-word contradiction gives the sampled line its force, following the suggestion to stop watching upsetting news.

sources.label: Ethel Cain recites the line in Genius Verified, 07:30

notes.title: Every little drop
notes.original: 点点滴滴 / 小心翼翼
notes.body: 点点滴滴 gathers the tiny, scattered details of life into one phrase; its repeated syllables make the accumulation audible. 小心翼翼 then means extremely carefully. The refrain treats everyday moments like fragile things that can be gathered and kept.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 點點滴滴
Ministry of Education dictionary: 小心翼翼

notes.title: The fruits of effort
notes.original: 一切果实都来自我自己
notes.body: 果实 means both literal fruit and the results earned through effort, much like 'the fruits of my labor.' The line claims those achievements as his own. The following lines shift their value toward the well-being of friends and family.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 果實

notes.title: 幸福 is a kind of well-being
notes.body: 幸福 is happiness understood as a good, fulfilling life, rather than only a passing cheerful mood. “Blessed” fits the gratitude and prayer around it, but the Chinese word itself does not specify a religious blessing. Friends and family doing well are the concrete measure of that happiness here.

notes.title: A shared future pictured as a scroll
notes.body: 画卷 is a pictorial scroll and, figuratively, an unfolding scene. Everyone’s name is written onto this one; the speaker will preserve it and make sure each person is looked after. The image changes private success into something deliberately kept for a whole circle of people. In a June 2025 interview about the earlier Above & Beyond, Jackzebra similarly described collecting producer friends into a picture album, with lyrics as his annotations. That earlier explanation offers a parallel to this image, rather than identifying the people in this song.

sources.label: Jackzebra on Above & Beyond, Sabukaru, June 2025

notes.title: Names worth preserving
notes.body: 芳名 can mean a good reputation or a person's name spoken with respect. Paired with 永存, 'endure forever,' it gives the blessing a ceremonial register. The friends and family just pictured together become people whose names deserve to last.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 芳名

notes.title: Monsters can also be human threats
notes.body: This four-part grouping piles up supernatural beings—demons, devils, ghosts, and monsters. It can also be used figuratively for sinister people or forces. Leaving it as creatures in English keeps the protective, almost spell-like form of the request without deciding which everyday dangers it means.

notes.title: The posture reverses the boast
notes.body: Here the speaker lowers himself to ask for protection for others. “Kai” later orders somebody else onto their knees; “Throat” returns to pleading before a Buddha. Kneeling changes meaning with who is speaking and who must kneel: devotion, dominance, and desperation are distinct uses across the mixtape.

notes.title: Prayer in the words and hands
notes.body: The pronoun changes to 您, the respectful form of 'you.' Just before it, 合十 describes palms and all ten fingers joined before the chest, a gesture of reverence with Buddhist associations. The paired verbs 祈祷 and 祷告 intensify the act of praying; the addressee remains unnamed.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 合十
Ministry of Education dictionary: 祈禱

phrase.en: pray to you, pray to you

notes.title: The teacher becomes a salesman
notes.body: Read in the voice of the teacher, this opening moves from discipline to coercion: bad grades bring threats, then survival is tied to paid Sunday lessons. The hourly rate punctures the grand language about an educational career. That turn gives the classroom scene its satirical bite.

notes.title: The discipline ruler
notes.body: 戒尺 is a ruler-like implement historically used by teachers to punish pupils. This one is described as iron. The following line specifies the palms and backs of the hands, making the classroom's authority physical and painful.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 戒尺

notes.title: Learning made physical
notes.body: 长记性 literally means to develop memory, but in a reprimand it means finally learning not to repeat a mistake. Coming immediately after the strikes to both sides of the hands, it turns “learning” into the memory of punishment rather than understanding a subject.

notes.title: The threat becomes an hourly charge
notes.body: 补课 can mean extra or make-up tuition outside ordinary classes. Here the teacher sends the pupil to the teacher’s own home, then immediately names an hourly charge and a monthly payment schedule. The promise of education is made inseparable from a private transaction.

notes.title: A schoolyard song with a dark second life
notes.body: The hook borrows from 上学歌, the Going to School Song, and its long-circulating playground parody. Chinese reporting described children singing the school-destruction version in 2007 and 2010. Recognizing that shared childhood joke changes the chorus from an isolated threat into a familiar singalong turned grotesque.

sources.label: 2007 school report on rewritten nursery songs
Zhengzhou Evening News / China News: playground parodies, 2010

notes.title: A schoolbag becomes an explosive
notes.body: The original school song sends a cheerful child off with a schoolbag; the parody swaps its contents for explosives and turns attendance into a fantasy of escape. Its destruction of the school overturns the obedient routine of the original.

sources.label: Zhengzhou Evening News / China News: the school-song rewrite

notes.title: The pupil’s rebellion starts giving orders

phrase.en: You've got to hear what I say

notes.body: The teacher begins by issuing commands and threats. After the school-song parody, the voice asks what could be forbidden, then commands the listener to hear and watch. The sequence makes rebellion take on the imperative form of the authority it has just attacked.

notes.title: An anatomical “eye”
notes.body: 马眼 literally says “horse eye,” but it is slang for the opening at the tip of the penis. “Pisshole” carries both the anatomy and the coarse register. Two lines earlier, 狗眼 is an insult directed at someone’s eyes; 马眼 repeats 眼 while moving to a different body part. The sequence then shifts into pixelation and an impossible autopsy.

sources.label: Urologist Li Hongjun: the anatomical meaning of 马眼

notes.title: A censored image after the threat
notes.body: 马赛克 literally means mosaic; in media language it also means pixelation used to obscure part of an image. The line turns the preceding violent image into something one cannot clearly see, before the next line says even an autopsy is impossible. It changes from bodily detail to the image that might be left on a screen.

notes.title: Calling it all discipline
notes.body: 统称 means grouping several things under one name. The refrain does more than name a subject: it labels what follows—rules, beatings, scolding and forced-looking behavior. 'We call it all discipline' preserves that act of naming, and the later verse supplies the explicit 'we.'

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 統稱

notes.title: Miracles leave; discipline stays
notes.body: Miracles are scarce, and then the magician goes home: the wording moves from something supernatural to somebody who performs illusions. What remains receives the name “discipline.” Read together, the lines let that tidy label replace any promise of transformation or rescue.

notes.title: People as loose sand
notes.body: Loose sand is an established idiom for people who cannot hold together as a group. Each grain remains separate. Placing it after 体系, 'system,' sets up the verse's tension: organization promises cohesion, while the next lines show the punishment used to enforce it.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 一片散沙

notes.title: A question across two lines
notes.body: The final 后 means 'after' and can carry the dream clause into the next question: 'After you dream about it in your sleep, wouldn't you be afraid?' The object of the dream is left unstated. This reading keeps the thought connected without inventing a particular nightmare.

notes.title: Keep going / fill the tank
notes.body: 加油 means adding fuel and is also the everyday cheer 'keep going!' or 'come on!' Here the question separates 油, 'fuel,' from 加, 'add.' The coming car scene makes refueling literal, while the encouragement meaning creates an uneasy echo beside the trembling legs.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 加油

notes.title: The spontaneous-trip slogan
notes.body: 说走就走的旅行 became a familiar phrase for the freedom to drop everything and travel; a 2015 China Tourism Academy speech discussed it as a youth buzzword. Here the passengers sit behind a driver who cannot see. The cheerful slogan lands inside a scene where they have little control over where they are going.

notes.title: A vulgar word used as a boast
notes.body: 屌 is profane, but as an adjective it can praise someone as formidable or impressive. “Badass or what?” keeps the boast and its rough register. Later, 草 functions as a sound-alike spelling of the swear 操, not as literal grass.

notes.title: Applause turns into a burial image
notes.body: Flowers and applause initially look like rewards for performing, but they already cover a body. The song later supplies a tombstone, coffin, and burial clothes. That sequence lets the same image move from public adoration toward a funeral, making success and disposal disturbingly close.

notes.title: A snack rhyme becomes a funeral sales pitch
notes.body: The pairing of “check it out” with 来一套 echoes the jianbing snack rhyme documented in this Nankai Youth League food article. Here the familiar order for a set is filled with a coffin and burial clothes. This identifies the textual resemblance, not a confirmed statement of the artist’s intent.

phrase.en: Yo, yo, yo, check it out

notes.title: The same character in two different transactions
notes.body: Earlier 戴套 means wearing a condom; here 一套 means a complete set. The character 套 links the sexualized exchange for money and fame to the sale of a coffin with burial clothes.

notes.title: A ritual turned into a performance insult
notes.body: 跳大神 names spirit-invoking ritual performance involving dancing and incantation, traditionally associated with seeking protection or driving away misfortune. The lyric adds an obscene performance instruction to it; “Kai” later uses the same expression inside its grotesque caveman image. That sacred-to-derisive shift matters more here than the literal act of dancing.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 跳大神

notes.title: Banknotes compared with school papers
notes.body: The gaokao is China’s national college entrance exam. A documented post-exam celebration involves throwing study materials into the air; this gives a concrete visual context for the preceding stacks of money flying. The photograph is contextual evidence, not the identified event behind the lyric.

sources.label: China Daily — students tossing study materials after the gaokao (2013)

notes.title: One more meaning of 套
notes.body: 套 has already appeared in 戴套, wearing a condom, and 一套, a complete set of funeral goods. 圈套 adds the sense of a trap or setup. This third use turns the repeated character into a chain connecting sex, sales, and manipulation.

notes.title: An unresolved source phrase
notes.body: The supplied Genius text reads “world / big straw hat.” The phrase is awkward in context and may need correction after listening. The English keeps the literal image and marks the uncertainty rather than replacing it with a more familiar saying.

phrase.en: The world's a giant straw hat

notes.title: Disgust has a literal smell
notes.body: 狗屁 literally means dog fart, but its ordinary insulting force is “nonsense” or “bullshit.” The Chinese animal-and-smell image becomes an English excrement idiom rather than a literal canine event. Repeating it after the grand claims of fame and praise collapses those claims into something worthless.

notes.body: 撑起一片天 pictures supporting a whole space above oneself. As a figurative phrase, it suggests taking responsibility or establishing a place where one can stand independently. Beside earning little but refusing deception, the boast concerns sustaining a life on one’s own terms.

notes.title: Face means dignity
notes.body: This is a variant of the proverb that people have faces as trees have bark: a person needs dignity and a sense of shame. Following the refusal to deceive for money, it makes 'face' a matter of self-respect. The title can therefore resonate with both facial expression and social standing.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 人有臉樹有皮

phrase.en: Trees need bark; people need their dignity

notes.title: Familiar—and cooked
notes.original: 这样不用社交软件就能自来熟
notes.body: 自来熟 describes someone who becomes familiar with strangers immediately. The pivot is 熟, which means both 'familiar' and 'cooked.' Put people in a boiling pot and they will get 'familiar' without a social app: the line makes a social idiom literal as a gruesome joke.

notes.title: No limit—and then a temperature
notes.body: 度 can mean a degree, a measure, or a proper limit. Here jokes have no 度; a few lines later 温度 explicitly names temperature, inside a sequence about boiling and heat. The same character links social restraint to the physically excessive cooking joke.

notes.title: Nothing left to fear
notes.body: A dead pig does not fear boiling water: the proverb describes someone hardened enough to be unafraid, often with a scornful sense of shamelessness. The lyric takes that stock saying back into the pot-and-cooking imagery, then follows it with another reference to heat.

sources.label: Hanzi dictionary: 死猪不怕開水燙

phrase.en: A dead pig that isn't scared of boiling water

notes.title: Swagger described from outside
notes.body: 装逼 means putting on airs or performing impressiveness, with a coarse, dismissive edge. Unlike 牛逼, praise for being formidable, it draws attention to the act of trying to look that way. “Wow” and “so cool” can therefore sound like either mock admiration or enjoyment of the pose, rather than simple endorsement.

notes.title: Designer names take the place of objects
notes.body: “Commes” plausibly points to Comme des Garçons, while the later “ricks” plausibly points to Rick Owens: fashion labels become shorthand for possessions inside the repeated “I got” inventory. The transcript does not identify particular garments or shoe models. These readings explain the likely brand shorthand while preserving the source spelling.

notes.title: YoungQueenz is OZMA
notes.body: OZMA is a name YoungQueenz uses on his own Bandcamp and SoundCloud pages. The guest verse's repeated 'young zeebra / young ozma' therefore names the collaborators, rather than introducing an unexplained third person. He closes with a compact reversal of a familiar idea: keeping going is easier than giving up.

notes.title: The easier choice is reversed

phrase.en: Keeping going is easier than giving up

notes.body: The expected motivational comparison makes perseverance harder and quitting easier. YoungQueenz reverses it: continuing is now the easier action. Beside the catalog of things he has and places he tours, the reversal sounds like momentum or commitment becoming habitual.

tracks.intro: Face as dignity, familiarity as cooking, and a proverb returned to boiling water. YoungQueenz enters under his OZMA name.

notes.body: This is a version of the familiar maxim 失败是成功之母: failure can lead to success. notes.title: Resignation inside the easy life

phrase.en: get by one day at a time

notes.body: 得过且过 means muddling through as long as one can, without ambitious plans or a strong sense of purpose. It often carries criticism of that attitude. “One day at a time” sounds gentler in English; the Chinese leaves more room for both deliberate ease and resignation.

notes.title: Company counted in bowls and chopsticks
notes.body: The refusal of extra company becomes a concrete domestic image: there are no spare place settings. No additional identity or relationship is assigned to the unnamed 她, “she,” in the preceding line.

notes.title: Being remembered is not always comforting
notes.body: 惦记 can mean keeping someone fondly in mind, worrying about them, or having one’s eye on something one wants. The surrounding refusal of extra company makes the attention unwelcome. English “thinking of me” preserves the openness of the word without deciding whether these people miss him or want something from him.

notes.title: The first half of a Buddhist saying
notes.body: The familiar saying continues with becoming a Buddha on the spot: even someone who has done wrong can turn toward good. The lyric stops after laying down the knife, then moves to being at ease and sleeping peacefully. A moral turning point becomes the threshold to an ordinary, restful life.

sources.label: Ministry of Education dictionary: 放下屠刀，立地成佛

notes.title: A duck in the title, a fish in the lyric
notes.body: The Chinese idiom is literally “like a fish getting water,” meaning being at ease in the right environment. The English title uses the related English image of a duck taking to water; the lyric translation keeps the fish.

notes.title: An intimate idiom applied to a pillow
notes.body: 如胶似漆 means stuck together like glue and lacquer, often describing an inseparable couple. Here it modifies a pillow, turning the bed into the object of that attachment.

notes.title: A source line to check against the audio
notes.body: The supplied community transcript reads 清先. That sequence is unusual here; the English renders the surrounding instruction while flagging the unresolved word rather than silently correcting the Chinese.

notes.title: The same two characters, reversed
notes.body: 错过 means to miss an opportunity; 过错 means a fault or wrongdoing. Reversing 错 and 过 creates the question-and-answer-like pair while changing the meaning.

notes.title: A meal stands for a livelihood
notes.body: 讨口饭 or 讨口饭吃 can mean scraping out a living. The small mouthful makes basic subsistence the scale of the effort. Beside the insistence on getting money and running, it keeps the cash imagery tied to survival as well as ambition.

notes.title: A weather forecast for a face
notes.body: 局部多云 is “partly cloudy,” the phrasing of a weather report. Applying it to 脸色, facial appearance or expression, turns a bad mood into a forecast.

notes.title: The sound of a clearance sale
notes.body: 全场清仓 and 大甩卖 are stock sales calls: everything must go, a huge clearance sale. The later 走过路过不要错过 is another call to passing customers, carried here into the surrounding personal imagery.

notes.title: The bait meets somebody who will not bite
notes.body: 老奸巨猾 describes someone deeply practiced in deceit or cunning. There is no fox in the Chinese; English supplies its own familiar animal for that character. With a loach held at the mouth in the previous line, 不会咬 works both as refusing food and refusing to be lured in.

notes.title: A hard mouth and an uneasy heart
notes.body: 嘴硬 is refusing to concede or continuing to talk tough despite contrary evidence. The next line’s 心虚 is inward unease, guilt, or lack of confidence. Together they split the person into a defiant mouth and an insecure interior; the praise of how “cool” and “beautiful” this looks carries a mocking edge.

notes.title: Grey is also something that covers you
notes.body: 灰 can mean dust or ash as a substance, and grey as a color. 一身灰 naturally pictures being covered in dust, which is how the translation reads it. The English title keeps the color available, so the ending joins a bodily coating to the song’s grey atmosphere.

notes.title: A soldier’s exterior without a battle

notes.title: One word moves from exhausted to destructive
notes.body: The opening’s 废 describes feeling useless or spent; 废了 here becomes something the speaker will do to other people’s mouths—ruin or disable them. The shared word converts a state of personal depletion into an outward threat, still directed at speech rather than an identified opponent.

notes.title: Huddling for warmth becomes a clique
notes.body: 抱团取暖 literally means grouping together for warmth. Beside 小圈子, a small circle or clique, it describes people sheltering and supporting one another within a closed group.

notes.title: Drunk with disbelief
notes.body: 我也是醉了 often expresses being speechless, exasperated, or overwhelmed by something absurd. The first-person admission need not report drinking. “I can’t even” aims to carry that exhausted reaction into English, alongside the verse’s claims of being worn out.

notes.title: A rich person—or a game?
notes.body: 大富翁 ordinarily means a very rich person, but it is also a name associated with property-trading board and computer games. The next line’s 防沉迷, preventing addictive absorption, makes a gaming reading possible alongside the insult. The unusual English title “Monoplay” may strengthen that association, but the transcript does not establish a specific game.

notes.title: A regional word for chili
notes.body: 海椒 is a regional name for chili peppers. The line puts it beside kangaroo meat; the translation retains that unusual pairing without assigning it an unverified travel story.

notes.title: A brand name that also sounds self-absorbed
notes.body: 自嗨锅 is the Zihaiguo brand of self-heating meals. Its name also contains 自嗨: entertaining oneself or getting excited in one’s own bubble. Calling the product expired, near the lines about little cliques, allows the food label to echo the surrounding criticism of closed, self-satisfied circles.

notes.title: The cover that hides disgrace
notes.body: 遮羞布 literally means a cloth for covering shame. Figuratively it is the excuse or respectable appearance that conceals something embarrassing or dishonorable. “Fig leaf” uses the English idiom for the same function; the Chinese does not specifically mention a leaf.

notes.title: Avoiding work by being clever about it
notes.body: 偷奸耍滑 describes using sly tricks to avoid effort or responsibility. It is not the same as the outright fraud in the parallel line about scams. Keeping the two accusations distinct makes the repeated contempt target both active deception and opportunistic evasion.

notes.title: Two lines that need an audio check
notes.original: 请了你最喜欢的固定资产
notes.body: 固定资产 is the ordinary accounting term “fixed assets,” making this line difficult to resolve in its funeral context. The earlier 脑瘤学生, literally “brain-tumor students,” is also unusual. Both are preserved and flagged, not repaired by guesswork.

notes.title: The last detail is who paid
notes.body: The threatening funeral scene ends with the same correction three times: the beloved people sent the wreath, but the speaker paid for it. The repetition makes the mundane payment detail the punchline.

notes.title: Posture as moral character
notes.body: 行得端、坐得正 is a declaration of upright conduct: one has done nothing shameful and can face scrutiny. The song splits it into two short lines after “stand high / see far,” making physical position and moral self-confidence share the same rhythm. The community spelling 的 is preserved.

notes.title: An unusual object in the transcript
notes.body: The source reads 大结果, literally “big result,” as something gripped in a hand. The English keeps that odd object instead of silently substituting a more plausible weapon or prize. This particular noun needs verification against the vocal.

notes.title: Selling a constructed self
notes.body: 人设 is a constructed persona or public character. 卖人设, literally “sell a persona,” accuses someone of marketing that image to an audience. The following fear of being forgotten makes attention itself part of the insult.

notes.title: Fragility you can poke through
notes.body: Traditional paper-covered windows supply a concrete image for the previous fragile self-esteem: one poke ruins the surface. The lyric moves directly from an abstract weakness to something that can be punctured.

notes.title: A bird that repeats human speech
notes.body: 八哥 is a myna, a bird known for imitating human speech. 碎嘴 means incessant, petty chatter. Together they reduce the opponent’s voice to tiresome repeated noise; the following charge that culture is “just talk” continues that attack on speech without substance.

sources.label: Taipei Zoo: mynas imitating human voices

notes.title: Shameless, not resilient
notes.body: 皮厚 draws on 脸皮厚, a thick face: being shameless or unembarrassed when one should feel ashamed. English “thick-skinned” can praise resilience, but that is not the force of this insult. The accusation sits beside fragile self-esteem, so outward shamelessness and inward insecurity coexist.

notes.title: Betrayal as a possessing spirit
notes.original: 背刺鬼半夜上身随手做做
notes.body: 背刺 is a stab in the back, and by extension betrayal. Adding 鬼 turns the betraying impulse into a ghost; 上身 says it possesses the body. 随手做做 then treats that dramatic supernatural intrusion as something done casually. The line moves between a familiar social metaphor and a little horror scene.

notes.title: A change in the food image
notes.body: 肉 is meat; 菜 can mean vegetables or a prepared dish, and in slang it can mean being bad at something. The literal food image is retained here. The next line gives up on playing, but the transcript alone does not establish which sense is intended.

phrase.en: The meat's turned into a dish

notes.title: No free pancakes from heaven
notes.body: The proverb says that stuffed pancakes do not fall from the sky: rewards do not simply arrive without effort. Keeping the food image preserves the abrupt shift from heaven’s will to practical advice about working and deciding for yourself.

After celebrating his own brothers’ good fortune, the speaker warns against granting that status freely. The following “sincerity doesn’t buy sincerity” questions whether the commitment will be returned.

notes.title: The family tree as a threat
notes.body: Claiming to be someone’s 祖宗, ancestor, is a way of asserting contemptuous superiority. 孙子, grandson, pushes the listener down the same hierarchy. The demanded 磕头 is a kneeling bow that brings the forehead to the ground, so the language of seniority becomes a physical demand for submission.

notes.title: A head underfoot, then a ball in play
notes.body: 运球 is the sporting action of moving with or dribbling a ball. Placed directly after stepping on someone’s head and before “life is like a game,” it lets humiliation slide into play. The sequence sustains control over the opponent while making the violence sound routine.

notes.title: A real appliance brand inside the threat
notes.body: 方太 is Fotile, a kitchen-appliance company that makes range hoods. After the pressure-cooker threat, the very specific product detail makes the imagined kitchen mundane and recognizable. It is a domestic brand mention, not the name of another person.

notes.title: Friends, tar and anxiety
notes.original: 交友不慎焦油里掺了点焦虑
notes.body: The sound runs from 交友 jiāoyǒu, making friends, to 焦油 jiāoyóu, tar, to 焦虑 jiāolǜ, anxiety. The first two are close in sound but very different in meaning; the shared 焦 keeps the chain moving. A literal English line preserves the bizarre mixture while this note restores the audible connection.

phrase.en: mixed a little anxiety into the tar

notes.title: Crying and “cool” share a sound
notes.original: 哭你妈逼是不是觉得自己很酷
notes.body: 哭 kū, “cry,” and 酷 kù, “cool,” differ only in tone. The taunt turns the opponent’s crying into a question about their pose, closing the line with almost the sound it began with. The English captures the challenge but loses that tight sound reversal.

notes.title: A street-level warning about fighting
notes.body: The win/lose construction echoes a widely used police warning: lose a fight and go to hospital; win and go to jail. This lyric uses “pay compensation” for the winning outcome. The next “I’m not afraid” answers the warning with bravado.

notes.title: A cheerful V at an enemy
notes.body: 比耶 means make the familiar two-finger V gesture used for photographs, victory or “peace.” It is a hand pose rather than merely saying “yeah.” A bright, camera-ready gesture arrives immediately after the warning about fighting, giving the confrontation a deliberately incongruous expression.

notes.title: An “eye” for other people’s motives
notes.body: 心眼 can mean shrewdness, suspicion or a calculating intention, as well as the capacity to judge people. 没有心眼 can praise someone’s straightforwardness or expose their naivety. The next lines deliberately provoke and trample others, complicating this claim to live innocently.

notes.title: A moral line becomes a painted line
notes.body: 底线 is a bottom line or limit one will not cross, including a moral boundary. Claiming blindness makes “where is the line?” into an excuse for not observing one. The verse then produces actual white lines on a road: the abstract limit leads into the crosswalk image.

notes.title: How paint makes a zebra
notes.original: 斑马斑马斑马斑马斑马斑马
notes.body: 斑马 means zebra, and 斑马线, “zebra lines,” is the everyday Chinese term for a crosswalk. The sequence paints white stripes on a street, lets them dry, then chants “zebra.” That also brings the artist’s own name into the refrain without having to say “Jack.”

notes.title: Money needs washing
notes.body: A washing machine follows the complaint about earning too much money. 洗钱 is the Chinese term for money laundering, literally “wash money”; putting an actual washer beside the money makes that figurative verb into a domestic appliance joke.

notes.title: Five A’s is an official tourism grade
notes.original: 目标是打造成著名的5A级景区
notes.body: 5A is the highest grade in China’s national tourist-attraction rating system. The line adopts development-plan language—“the goal is to build”—then follows it with a formal welcome to auspicious land. The precise grade gives the grand promise the sound of tourism promotion.

sources.label: Ministry of Culture and Tourism: 5A is the highest grade

notes.title: From official welcome to notification
notes.original: 您有一笔待接收的转账
notes.body: The polite 您 and “a transfer waiting to be accepted” read like a payment notification. 举报 then abruptly turns reception into a complaint: the money is only game currency. The short labels 报告, 提醒, 举报 and 遗言 make the verse keep changing its format, from report to alert to accusation to last words.

notes.body: 盘核桃 means handling and rolling ornamental walnuts, often a matched pair, so their shells develop a patina over time. These are objects to fiddle with and collect. Together with the fan and security booth, the action gives the refrain a concrete routine of passing time.

notes.title: The big share and the small share
notes.body: 大头 and 小头 literally mean “big head” and “small head,” but here mean the larger and smaller portions of money. Most is saved for the future; the remainder meets 温饱, the basic needs of food and clothing. Translating them as body parts would obscure this ordinary budgeting vocabulary.

notes.title: Drifting gives way to confrontation
notes.body: The opening wants an empty mind, a bed and nothing to do. After the clipped list of bad moods, the text turns outward toward unreliable people and ends with repeated threats. That change in addressee—from describing “I” to challenging “you”—drives the song’s movement.

notes.title: A stance of not taking things seriously
notes.body: 吊儿郎当 describes a careless, unserious way of behaving, often with a judgment that someone is shirking responsibility. Here the speaker adopts that description himself and immediately says it feels great. It makes the opening’s inactivity sound like an embraced attitude rather than just a lack of energy.

notes.title: A warm face meets a cold backside
notes.body: 热脸贴冷屁股 describes offering warmth or eagerness and getting cold indifference in return. Its deliberately undignified body image makes the effort look humiliating. The English keeps the image so the rejection remains as coarse as the Chinese.

notes.title: A baffling “move”
notes.body: 操作 means an operation or the way someone handles something. Calling it 谜一般, “like a mystery,” is a sarcastic way to say someone’s behavior makes no sense. “Move” carries that judgment without suggesting a medical operation.

notes.title: A hidden motive, pictured inside the body
notes.body: 心怀鬼胎 literally imagines harboring a ghostly fetus in one’s heart. As an idiom it means concealing a bad intention or ulterior motive. “Something to hide” carries the accusation; it is not a literal pregnancy or supernatural event.

notes.title: Words that do not count as a promise
notes.body: 说话算话 means that what you say counts: you keep your promises. Negating it repeats 话, “words,” around the failure to follow through. The later demand for 真心话, honest words, tightens the complaint from unreliability into a test of sincerity.

notes.title: Nothing left to take

phrase.en: Money? Got none—just one worthless life

notes.body: The defiant formula 要钱没有，要命一条 offers a life when there is no money to hand over. Adding 烂, “rotten” or “worthless,” makes even that last stake sound devalued. It is both self-dismissal and a refusal to be intimidated.

notes.title: Two sets of behavior

phrase.en: One face to me, another behind my back

notes.body: Literally one set in front of someone and another behind their back: a familiar accusation of hypocrisy. 套 refers to a whole pattern of behavior, connecting this complaint with the album’s recurring distrust of 套路, practiced routines or tricks.

notes.title: A pie made of promises
notes.body: 画饼 (“draw a pie”) means holding out attractive promises that may never materialize. Saying he still has not eaten turns that empty promise back into literal food.

phrase.en: Paint me a bigger pie, bigger still

notes.title: Mock sweetness
notes.body: 宝子 is an affectionate, informal address derived from 宝贝, “darling.” Dropped into the request for ever bigger empty promises, it makes the encouragement sound teasing or sarcastic rather than sincerely trusting.

notes.title: An unresolved English fragment
notes.body: The community source gives “crack rn” in the mixed-language line. Its intended grammar and sense are unclear, so the draft retains it rather than inventing a correction.

notes.title: A vulgar compliment
notes.body: 屌 is a vulgar anatomical word that also works as slang for impressive, formidable, or awesome. Here it praises his own style. Translating the anatomical meaning literally would miss the boast, while “good” alone would lose its register.

notes.title: Giving face
notes.body: 给脸 means showing someone respect or giving them room to behave honorably. Saying they refuse it is an insult: they have rejected the consideration offered.

notes.title: Moments
notes.body: Literally “circle of friends,” this is WeChat’s social feed, commonly called Moments in English. His feed and contact list become the stage for the final exaggerated announcement.

notes.title: Choosing ordinary appetites

phrase.en: worldly person—greedy for money, hungry for sex

notes.body: 俗人 places the speaker among worldly, ordinary people rather than someone above material desires. 贪财好色 openly embraces two conventionally criticized appetites, money and sex. After the advice about sleep, food, and staying alive, the line makes pleasure an unapologetic small-scale life philosophy.

notes.title: An instinctive writing process

phrase.en: A song every half hour on average

notes.body: The boast fits his account of writing in response to beats: in i-D he describes ordinary life as inspiration and says the beat prompts what he writes. That gives context for the casual recording scene, without treating “half an hour” as a verified production average.

notes.title: Calling his own singing a racket
notes.body: 鬼哭狼嚎 is a set expression for terrible wailing or howling, literally ghosts crying and wolves howling. Applying it to his own late-night recording makes the claim that music is easy self-mocking as well as boastful.

notes.title: Reading out the names

notes.title: A phonetic profanity
notes.body: 麻痹 literally refers to numbness or paralysis, but this construction uses its sound as a stand-in for a coarse insult. Reading it medically would miss the opening’s aggressive invitation to get up and party.

notes.title: Talking battles on paper
notes.body: Literally discussing military strategy on paper. The idiom criticizes abstract talk with no practical ability behind it; the following official-sounding declarations become examples.

notes.title: A comments section speaks like a ministry
notes.body: “Strongly condemn” and the following “solemnly protest” are formulas used in official diplomatic statements. Putting them after flooding a social feed makes the online outburst sound comically state-like. The cited statement demonstrates the register; the lyric does not name its particular dispute.

sources.label: Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs: example of both formulas

notes.title: Fooling ghosts
notes.body: Literally “are you fooling ghosts?”—a dismissive way of saying nobody would believe this. The repeated 鬼 also connects the chorus to the ghosts and devils in the guest verse.

phrase.en: Who do you think you're fooling

notes.title: The country-escape catchphrase

phrase.en: Too many scams in the city—I'm going back to the countryside

notes.body: This recalls the circulated saying 城市套路深，我要回农村: the city’s tricks run deep, so I’m returning to the countryside. A 2016 Xinhua report already described it as a popular phrase. Chun immediately punctures the escape fantasy with the muddy road’s holes and traps.

sources.label: Xinhua report on the circulated phrase, via People’s Daily

notes.title: Holes and traps
notes.body: 坑 can be a literal pit or a figurative trap or scam. Returning to muddy rural roads does not escape the city’s 套路, its tricks and schemes.

notes.title: How many floors?
notes.body: The community text prints 建基层, roughly “build the base level.” This translation reads it as a likely transcription of 建几层, “build how many floors”: 几层 and 基层 sound very similar. That is an editorial reading, not an audio-verified correction; the printed Chinese is preserved. The later line beginning 我祈求 also has an abrupt pronoun shift, retained in the English.

phrase.en: how many floors your tower has

notes.title: A belly between you and a heart

phrase.en: You can't see inside people's hearts

notes.body: Literally, the heart is separated from view by the belly’s skin. The saying means someone’s intentions cannot be known from the outside. Pairing it with acting tough online questions the reliability of the persona on display.

notes.title: The awkward bird gets an early start
notes.body: This proverb says that a less gifted person can compensate by starting earlier and working harder. The added image of being covered in excrement abruptly soils the familiar encouragement; the slow bird is neither elegant nor triumphant.

notes.title: An old-fashioned address
notes.body: 娘子 is an older form of address for a woman or wife. Here it gives the repeated romantic call a theatrical, old-fashioned flavor amid the much rougher talk about money, ambition, and confrontation.

notes.title: A “teacher” of fate
notes.body: 老师 can be an honorific for a practitioner, not only a schoolteacher. The fortune-teller’s call is later answered by 改命, changing fate, and the boast that Chun’s progress did not depend on a master. The verse sets prediction against making one’s own way.

notes.title: A film-star comparison
notes.body: Fan Bingbing is a Chinese actor and producer. Calling the woman “my Fan Bingbing” borrows a recognizable screen-star image as a personal comparison; it does not identify the woman as the celebrity herself.

sources.label: San Sebastián Festival: Fan Bingbing biography

notes.title: An aggressive “I”
notes.body: 老子 here is a swaggering, confrontational way of referring to oneself, roughly “your old man” used as “I.” It is not a reference to the philosopher Laozi. English distributes the aggression into “fucking” instead of translating the kinship term literally.

notes.title: Family and factory speech
notes.body: 老汉 can mean “Dad” in regional speech. Nearby, 打螺丝 literally means fastening screws and commonly evokes repetitive factory work; 黑中介 is an unscrupulous intermediary or broker.

notes.title: A nail in the eye
notes.body: The Chinese idiom names a nail in the eye: someone so resented that one wants them removed. English’s familiar “thorn in your side” transfers the meaning but softens the original location, which belongs to this verse’s unusually bodily language.

notes.title: A knife made into a verb
notes.body: 刀 (“knife”) is used as a verb here, conveying stabbing or attacking someone with a knife. The translation keeps the violent image rather than treating it as a neutral argument.

notes.body: 分寸 is the proper degree, limit, or tact a situation calls for; 拿捏 is managing it precisely. The boast is about calibrated judgment, not just physical balance, and the next lines recast that judgment as practiced muscle memory.

notes.title: A practiced hand
notes.body: 老师傅 is a respectful term for an experienced craftsperson or skilled worker. It emphasizes competence acquired through practice. Alongside muscle memory and the chessboard, it presents ability as something already lodged in the body and planned in advance.

notes.title: A place out of the wind
notes.body: A sheltered basin where boats can take refuge from wind and storms. The image gives years of solitary travel a possible destination: somewhere protected enough to stop.

notes.title: A body that cannot be written off
notes.body: 报废 is the word for retiring machinery, vehicles, or equipment as unusable. Applied to the tired speaker, it makes giving up feel like being removed from service before the effort invested in him has paid off.

notes.title: Effort with a life at stake
notes.body: 拼命 can mean trying with everything one has, literally putting one’s life on the line. “Sweet” later says 没必要拼命, that such expenditure is unnecessary. The phrase traces a tension between compulsive effort and the wish to stop sacrificing oneself.

notes.title: Firm tofu
notes.body: 老豆腐 means firm tofu, not spoiled or stale tofu. The whiteness, firmness, and resistance to falling apart extend his claims of a clean conscience and durability.

notes.title: His way of doing things
notes.body: 道 can be a road, a way, or a guiding method. The next line asks how anyone will block it, keeping the physical road inside the assertion of an independent way of living; the wording alone does not require a specific religious reading.

notes.title: An unsettled account
notes.body: 帐 is an account or ledger entry. Saying this account is not finished turns a grievance into something still owed between people. “Settling a score” preserves the same transfer from bookkeeping to conflict.

notes.title: A dangerous invitation
notes.body: The Hongmen Banquet in Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian involved a plot to kill Liu Bang during a feast hosted by Xiang Yu. The name now signals an invitation hiding hostile intentions; “acting skills” makes the politeness sound performed.

notes.title: Love of country as a ledger

phrase.en: Who dares say I don't love China

notes.body: The challenge is answered with taxes, spending earnings at home, funding a show, and covering travel costs. That accounting turns the abstract accusation into a list of concrete contributions. The lyric stages a defense against a charge; it does not itself identify who made that charge.

notes.title: Flights and hotels
notes.body: A compact abbreviation: 机 points to air travel and 酒 to 酒店, a hotel. Here 报 is read as covering or reimbursing those costs. The 20,000 in the preceding line has no currency specified in the text.

notes.title: An unresolved target
notes.body: The wording is literally “music uncle’s root and stem.” It may carry a phallic insult, but the lyric text alone does not establish who “music uncle” refers to. The translation keeps the odd image instead of assigning a name.

notes.title: Scolding the scolders
notes.body: 成何体统 is a formal, indignant rebuke: how can this be considered proper conduct? Put after mock titles like “great philosophical leader,” it lets the speaker imitate the elevated, disciplinary voice of the people he is taunting.

notes.title: Thunder without rain
notes.body: An idiom for loud promises, threats, or fuss followed by little action: much thunder, little rain.

phrase.en: lots of thunder and hardly any rain

notes.title: A taunt disguised as encouragement

phrase.en: Make sure you try harder in your next life

notes.body: The apparently encouraging wording becomes cruel by postponing the chance to improve until another lifetime. After “Die mad” and before “my insecure little darlings,” the sweetness is sarcastic; it need not express a literal belief in reincarnation.

notes.title: Influence recast as missionary work
notes.body: 传教 literally means spreading a religion. Used for the culture these rivals consume, it casts their supposedly authoritative taste as received doctrine. 糟粕, “dregs,” then dismisses what they have inherited as the discarded residue.

notes.title: His own complaint about overreading

phrase.en: reading a bit too much into it

notes.body: In STATIC, Jackzebra objects to accounts that turn his music into elaborate statements about Chinese society and says some descriptions overcomplicate it. That makes this complaint recognizable in his public outlook, while the specific addressee of the song remains unnamed.

notes.title: Faces and hidden knives
notes.body: 两面三刀 is an idiom for duplicity: presenting different faces, flattering someone while scheming against them. Its knife image sharpens the move from mocking foolish critics to accusing them of betrayal.

notes.title: A nationally charged insult
notes.body: 汉奸 is more charged than an ordinary personal traitor: it accuses someone of betraying China or Chinese people for an outside interest. The surrounding patriotic challenge makes that national frame essential to the insult, even in this exaggerated comparison.

notes.title: A possible Pocket Monsters wink

phrase.en: stuff them all in my pocket

notes.body: The adjacent “little creatures” and putting them all in a pocket can suggest Pokémon, whose Japanese title is Pocket Monsters and whose games center on collecting creatures. If read that way, the foolish antagonists become a collection of usable inspiration. The allusion is possible, not confirmed.

notes.title: The elevated family of China
notes.body: 华夏 is a literary-cultural name for China, and 儿女 makes belonging a family relationship. This grand register immediately gives way to calling someone a pig, before the old same-root verse returns to shared kinship. The shifts make national solidarity and personal abuse rub against each other.

notes.title: Born from one root
notes.body: These closing lines quote the Seven-Step Poem, traditionally attributed to Cao Zhi. In the poem, beanstalks fuel the fire cooking beans from the same root: an image of kin harming kin. Coming after 华夏儿女 (“children of China”), the quotation turns that shared origin toward the people he is addressing.

notes.title: Taking notes on ordinary life
notes.body: Jackzebra told i-D that inspiration comes from ordinary life, down to waking and meals. Describing Above & Beyond to Sabukaru, he compared its producers and beats to a picture album and his lyrics to annotations. “Trainee reporter” offers a similarly modest role: recording experience, not pronouncing a grand theory.

notes.title: The same word for formulas and scams
notes.body: 套路 can be an established sequence, a formula, or a manipulative routine. “Ghost Dog” uses it for distrusted social tricks; here it sits beside repeated melodies. The repeated word draws musical predictability and familiar social behavior into the same complaint.

notes.title: An easy ascent that still leaves wealth distant
notes.body: Immediately after denying shortcuts and a one-step arrival at the summit, the lyric puts people in an elevator looking toward faraway wealth. The mechanical way upward does not close the distance. It is a compact image of aspiration without arrival.

notes.title: A mirror that exposes monsters
notes.body: A magical mirror that reveals a disguised spirit’s true form, and a figurative device for exposing what someone really is. He turns it toward himself, making self-recognition more useful than looking farther or more closely at others.

notes.title: Time boils the rain
notes.body: This phrase is also the title of a song associated with Yisa Yu (郁可唯). The wording suggests a possible musical echo; Jackzebra does not identify a singer or recording in the line, so the connection remains an inference.

notes.title: A life reduced to a swipe

phrase.en: One swipe of a thumb and it's gone

notes.body: The long sequence of work, ambition, and disappointment shrinks to the tiny motion of a thumb. Read as the gesture of scrolling, it lets someone else pass over an entire emotional cycle almost instantly. The mismatch in scale gives the line its sting.

notes.title: Playing after insisting on first place
notes.body: Only a few lines earlier, he refuses to surrender the number-one spot. Now he proposes treating it as play and avoiding self-sacrifice. Those incompatible instructions can be heard as the competitive drive arguing with the need to protect himself from it.

notes.title: Immortal as a laughingstock
notes.body: Usually an approving expression for a name living on in history. Pairing it with 笑柄 (“laughingstock”) turns lasting fame into lasting embarrassment.

notes.title: Answering an older title
notes.body: Zhang Chu has a song titled 孤独的人是可耻的 (“Lonely people are shameful”). This passage appears to answer that wording: it repeatedly denies the shame, then changes the final response to “great.” The connection is a textual reading, not a confirmed statement of intent.

notes.title: Talking to himself, then out of words
notes.body: 无语 is often a colloquial expression of exasperation or disbelief, not physical inability to speak. It also repeats 语, “speech,” from the preceding 自语, talking to oneself: he keeps narrating his experience while finding it impossible to answer.

notes.title: What recognition adds
notes.body: In STATIC, he describes the period of making 王中王 as unusually free and says the later Hunched Jack came with more pressure. That account gives concrete career context for audience expectations becoming an invisible burden here, without making the verse a dated diary entry.

notes.title: From knowing everything to trusting ignorance
notes.body: Near the beginning he says he knows everything that is going on. The ending repeatedly places faith in not knowing. Across this long song, knowledge changes from a claim of mastery into something he may want relief from.
